notes.reason: This is Rees-Mogg's own advice, given as the closing tip of a video titled 'How to avoid paying the TV Licence fee legally': 'If you watch television on an iPhone and it is running on its battery, you do not need a TV license. So you can watch it wherever you are. The license relates to the property, not to the person. So you could be at a friend's house who hasn't got a license and you can watch a battery powered device without a license.' He repeats the point three more times, so no caption mishearing is possible. The note is correct. The battery rule is a term of a licence someone already holds, not an exemption: Schedule 1 of the Communications (Television Licensing) Regulations 2004 says a licence for a set of premises also covers 'the use anywhere of any television receiver powered solely by its own internal batteries' by the licensee or people living with them, and TV Licensing's own pages say you 'will be covered by your home TV Licence' when watching away from home on such a device. Both accepted gov.uk quotes are on the page, including the students' rule that lets them use the licence at their out-of-term address, and both MoneySavingExpert quotes are verbatim, including 'watching live TV on a phone requires a licence (though if you already have a licence at your home address you won't need an additional one for a mobile device used outside the home)'. So a viewer who follows his advice to drop the licence and watch live TV or his GB News hour live on a battery-powered phone is breaking the law, which is the opposite of what he promises ('I want you to obey the law'). That makes the correction substantive, not pedantic. He prides himself on the black letter of the legislation and the point is not political, so he could accept it, though he may not enjoy a correction to the one 'trap' he warned viewers about.
